issue_context.title: Enable tests that require exclusive access to hardware to be run without the exclusive tag.
issue_context.body:
### Description of the feature request:


In OpenTitan, we use bazel to coordinate and direct tests, and we have long running tests on simulators and on FPGAs. The FPGA tests require exclusive access to attached FPGAs, but don't conflict with any of the non-FPGA actions in our WORKSPACE.
https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/pull/16785 and it's predecessors offer a means to introduce extra resources like our fpga boards and issue tests in parallel with other actions, but without issuing multiple tests that require the FPGAs.

I can't find an open issue referenced in this work so I'm writing it up

### What underlying problem are you trying to solve with this feature?


We're trying to make our WORKSPACE aware of resource limitations that aren't covered by the CPU/Memory limits and aren't covered by "exclusive" tags or controlling the number of jobs without incurring a large overhead.

### Which operating system are you running Bazel on?


Rolling debian testing Rodette

### What is the output of `bazel info release`?


release 5.3.2

### If `bazel info release` returns `development version` or `(@non-git)`, tell us how you built Bazel.


_No response_

### What's the output of `git remote get-url origin; git rev-parse master; git rev-parse HEAD` ?


```text
https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel
d2aaf0cd66f10745aedee16330c2c053b848a507
ea1646d8d58f5252e55bb891b5eaee67778f23c7
```


### Have you found anything relevant by searching the web?

More discussion here: https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/pull/16785

### Any other information, logs, or outputs that you want to share?

_No response_

review_comments: You could use groups in the pattern to avoid having to split the result later. You could also make the regexp only match floats for the second part, though I don't know if that would make for worse errors.

I'd prefer not to do this:
This would require modification to the `ParseableRequirement create` method above, which assumes a single group is matched. My inclination is to keep this PR as small as possible.
@larsrc-google is this acceptable? Was your suggestion phrased this way to be polite? Is it resolved by my expressed preference here?
You're right, changing that would be overkill.
Shouldn't this be enforced in the ResourceManager?
I can't think of a reason this should be structured differently from the CPU tag check above.

To follow up and try to make progress here: Was this phrased as a question to be polite and this wont get merged if I don't do it? or is it a question that can be resolved by my preference not to do it?
No, it's fine to leave it the way you did it here.
If we have same entry multiple time then we return an error here. Let's do it more gracefully with more context.

I can't tell what you mean here. If I specify the local resources twice I don't see a problem:
```
# Allow bazel to allocate tests to 1 cw310 board.
test --local_extra_resources=cw310=1
test --local_extra_resources=cw310=1
test --local_extra_resources=cw310=2
```
Seems to work fine

`(v1,v2) -> v1` is different from how most options are handled where values can't be overridden. I'll change that to: `(v1,v2) -> v2` so args can override rc files and the priorities apply properly.

We could use min of v1 and v2 if that's acceptable instead.
Advantages:

- deterministic (doesn't depend on order)
- good reflection of intent as expressed by configuration

Disadvantages

- Less flexible,
- Inconsistent with other argument applications where subsequent expression of the same arg override defaults.

PLMK and I could change it.

Yes, .rc files are applied in order, before command-line flags. Using the first value is definitely bad. I can see arguments for both using the last one (allows easy override with what's really the case for the user) and using minimum (allows a group-wide max). Using the last one fits better with the usual Bazel behaviour, and since there's no enforcement of using a .rc file, it's pretty easy to (intentionally or accidentally) not use the group-wide max. So I would go for using the last.
We really should check that these are >= 0, lest somebody accidentally create resources out of thin air.
